what: RingCentral provides business phone and communication systems delivered over the internet. Instead of a company owning telephone equipment, RingCentral runs the calling, messaging, video meetings and contact centre software in its own data centres and charges per user per month.
customers: Businesses of all sizes replacing traditional phone systems, from small firms buying online to large enterprises with thousands of users and contact centres, often sold through partners including telecom carriers.
money: Per-user monthly fees for phone, messaging, video and contact centre services.
Hardware, professional services and usage charges.
moat: A company’s phone numbers and communication system are embedded in how it operates — on business cards, in customer records, in every process that involves calling someone. Migrating is disruptive enough that most firms do it once a decade. RingCentral also sells through carrier partners who bring customers it would not reach alone.
risks: Reported net income of $662.4M against a 1.7% net margin indicates a large one-off item, so the price/earnings ratio of 8.9 is not comparable to a normal year’s earnings.
Microsoft includes calling in Teams subscriptions customers already pay for, which is the hardest competitive problem in software.
Revenue growth has slowed sharply, from $1.6B in 2021 to $2.5B in 2025 but with the recent increments much smaller.
Debt of $1.3B against $132.6M of cash is meaningful for a company whose growth has decelerated.
Fourteen analysts average a $97.86 target against a $67.26 price, a 46% gap that reflects disagreement about whether growth stabilises.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $667.2M on $2.6B of revenue is substantial, and the shares trade at about 8.5 times it.
An installed phone system is genuinely difficult to displace, which protects the existing revenue base.
The contact centre product sells at higher prices per user than basic calling and is a larger addressable market.
Carrier partnerships distribute the product to customers RingCentral could not reach directly.
Revenue has grown every year shown, and the business converts it to cash efficiently.
watch: Annual recurring revenue growth and net retention, excluding the accounting noise. The question is whether existing customers are expanding or merely renewing, and the earnings line will not tell you.
view: RingCentral is in the position software companies dread: selling a product Microsoft includes for free in something customers already buy. Teams has calling, and for a great many businesses that is sufficient. RingCentral’s answer is that it does telephony properly — reliability, regulatory compliance, carrier-grade quality, contact centre depth — and for businesses where the phone is how they make money, that distinction is real. For businesses where the phone is a convenience, it is not.

Before anything else, discard the earnings figure. Reported net income of $662 million against a 1.7% net margin on $2.6 billion of revenue is incoherent on its face; a one-off item is doing the work, and the 8.9 times price/earnings ratio means nothing. The honest number is $667 million of free cash flow, which the shares trade at about 8.5 times. That is a cheap multiple for a business generating that much cash, and the cheapness is the market’s verdict on where growth is going.

The growth deceleration is the whole argument. Revenue went from $1.6 billion to $2.5 billion, but the recent annual increments are much smaller than the earlier ones, which is what a business looks like when the easy replacement cycle is done and the remaining prospects are harder to win. The contact centre product is the right strategic response — higher price per user, larger market, less directly in Microsoft’s path — and whether it works is the single open question.

What makes the stock interesting rather than simply cheap is that the installed base is genuinely sticky. A company’s phone numbers sit in its customer records, on its invoices, in every process involving a call; migrating is a project people do once a decade. So the existing revenue is reasonably safe and the cash flow is real. At 8.5 times free cash flow with $1.3 billion of debt, you are being paid to accept that the growth may be over. Net retention is the number that settles whether it is — expansion within existing customers, not new logos, is where a business in this position either survives or slowly stops.
bull: The contact centre product lifts revenue per user while a sticky installed base holds, and 8.5 times free cash flow turns out to price a stable business as a dying one.
bear: Teams is good enough for more customers each renewal, growth goes to zero, and $1.3 billion of debt sits against a shrinking revenue line.
